claim: Inhibition of OxPhos in neural stem cells (NSCs) or tumours in the Drosophila brain decreases proliferation.
source: We found that inhibition of OxPhos in neural stem cells (NSCs) or tumours in the Drosophila brain not only decreases proliferation, but also affects many different aspects of stem cell behaviour.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, and it is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: OxPhos dysfunction in NSCs leads to a protracted G1/S-phase.
source: In NSCs, OxPhos dysfunction leads to a protracted G1/S-phase and results in delayed temporal patterning and reduced neuronal diversity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Fly-FUCCI data in the manuscript.

claim: OxPhos dysfunction in NSCs results in delayed temporal patterning and reduced neuronal diversity.
source: In NSCs, OxPhos dysfunction leads to a protracted G1/S-phase and results in delayed temporal patterning and reduced neuronal diversity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunostaining data for temporal markers.

claim: NSCs with OxPhos dysfunction fail to undergo terminal differentiation, leading to prolonged neurogenesis into adulthood.
source: As a consequence, NSCs fail to undergo terminal differentiation, leading to prolonged neurogenesis into adulthood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing NSCs persisting in adult brains.

claim: In brain tumours, inhibition of OxPhos slows proliferation and prevents differentiation, resulting in reduced tumour heterogeneity.
source: Similarly, in brain tumours inhibition of OxPhos slows proliferation and prevents differentiation, resulting in reduced tumour heterogeneity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data on tumour growth and Imp expression.

claim: Some cancer cells rely primarily on aerobic glycolysis for energy and biomass production (the Warburg effect).
source: The observation that some cancer cells rely primarily on aerobic glycolysis for energy and biomass production (the Warburg effect) (Vander Heiden et al., 2009; Warburg, 1956) has often led to the assumption that the other main source of ATP, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos), is dispensable.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Many tumours require mitochondrial activity for energy and biosynthesis.
source: However, it is becoming increasingly clear that many tumours do require mitochondrial activity for energy and biosynthesis and OxPhos is now frequently exploited as a therapeutic target in cancer (Gui et al., 2016; Molina et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2019; Weinberg and Chandel, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: OxPhos is frequently exploited as a therapeutic target in cancer.
source: However, it is becoming increasingly clear that many tumours do require mitochondrial activity for energy and biosynthesis and OxPhos is now frequently exploited as a therapeutic target in cancer (Gui et al., 2016; Molina et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2019; Weinberg and Chandel, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature on cancer therapeutics.

claim: OxPhos takes place at the inner mitochondrial membrane in five large protein complexes (Complex I-V).
source: OxPhos takes place at the inner mitochondrial membrane in five large protein complexes (Complex I-V), which together form the respiratory chain.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cellular respiration.

claim: Complexes I-IV transfer electrons from NADH to O2 and use the released energy to translocate protons from the mitochondrial matrix into the intermembrane space.
source: Complexes I-IV transfer electrons from NADH to O2 and use the released energy to translocate protons from the mitochondrial matrix into the intermembrane space.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the electron transport chain.

claim: Complex V (ATP synthase) uses the electrochemical gradient to generate ATP from ADP.
source: The resulting electrochemical gradient is then used by Complex V (ATP synthase) to generate ATP from ADP.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ATP synthesis.

claim: OxPhos is directly involved in the generation of NAD+, orotate, fumarate and reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Apart from the production of ATP, OxPhos is also directly involved in the generation of NAD+, orotate, fumarate and reactive oxygen species (ROS) and thus affects many cellular processes, such as nucleotide synthesis (Birsoy et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2018; Sullivan et al., 2015), signalling pathway activity (Chandel, 2014) and epigenetic modifications (Lu and Thompson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature on mitochondrial metabolism.

claim: The Warburg effect has been interpreted as a normal adaptation to the metabolic requirements of proliferation, both in cancer cells and proliferating stem cells.
source: The Warburg effect has since been interpreted as a normal adaptation to the metabolic requirements of proliferation, both in cancer cells and proliferating stem cells (Vander Heiden et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on cancer metabolism.

claim: High glycolytic flux is thought to be required for a constant supply of biomass.
source: High glycolytic flux is thought to be required for a constant supply of biomass while OxPhos, apart from its role in production of ATP, primarily maintains the cellular redox balance (Birsoy et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2015; Titov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on cellular metabolism.

claim: OxPhos primarily maintains the cellular redox balance.
source: High glycolytic flux is thought to be required for a constant supply of biomass while OxPhos, apart from its role in production of ATP, primarily maintains the cellular redox balance (Birsoy et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2015; Titov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on cellular metabolism.

claim: Metabolic flux in cancer cells can be influenced by substrate availability, oncogenic mutations and the tumour's tissue and cell type of origin.
source: However, metabolic flux in cancer cells can be influenced by extrinsic and intrinsic factors such as substrate availability, oncogenic mutations and the tumour's tissue and cell type of origin (Hu et al., 2013; Mayers et al., 2016; Vander Heiden and DeBerardinis, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on cancer metabolism.

claim: Brain tumours recapitulate many features of their tissue of origin and grow along a hierarchy reminiscent of normal brain development.
source: Brain tumours in particular recapitulate many features of their tissue of origin and grow along a hierarchy reminiscent of normal brain development (Azzarelli et al., 2018; Genovese et al., 2018; Lan et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2018; Tiberi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature on brain tumours.

claim: The CNS of Drosophila develops from rapidly cycling embryonic and larval neural stem cells (NSCs) that generate a wide variety of neurons and glia.
source: The CNS of Drosophila develops from rapidly cycling embryonic and larval neural stem cells (NSCs) that generate a wide variety of neurons and glia.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Neuronal diversity in Drosophila is achieved primarily by spatial and temporal patterning.
source: Neuronal diversity is achieved primarily by spatial and temporal patterning, which confers specific identities on NSCs and their progeny according to their location and developmental time (Miyares and Lee, 2019; Technau et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on Drosophila development.

claim: Neural stem cells (NSCs) in Drosophila and mammals are thought to generate ATP through aerobic glycolysis rather than OxPhos.
source: Neural stem cells (NSCs) in Drosophila and mammals are thought to generate ATP through aerobic glycolysis rather than OxPhos, whereas their neuronal progeny switch to mitochondrial respiration upon differentiation (Agathocleous et al., 2012; Beckervordersandforth et al., 2017; Hall et al., 2012; Homem et al., 2014; Lange et al., 2016; Tennessen et al., 2014; Tennessen et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature on NSC metabolism.

claim: Neuronal progeny of NSCs switch to mitochondrial respiration upon differentiation.
source: Neural stem cells (NSCs) in Drosophila and mammals are thought to generate ATP through aerobic glycolysis rather than OxPhos, whereas their neuronal progeny switch to mitochondrial respiration upon differentiation (Agathocleous et al., 2012; Beckervordersandforth et al., 2017; Hall et al., 2012; Homem et al., 2014; Lange et al., 2016; Tennessen et al., 2014; Tennessen et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature on neuronal metabolism.

claim: Upregulation of aerobic glycolysis has been described in a number of Drosophila tumour paradigms.
source: Upregulation of aerobic glycolysis, reminiscent of the Warburg effect, has also been described in a number of Drosophila tumour paradigms (Eichenlaub et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2016; Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on Drosophila tumour models.

claim: The interpretation that mitochondrial respiration is dispensable for normal Drosophila NSCs contrasts with the clear requirement for OxPhos to support cell cycle progression in the Drosophila eye disc.
source: However, the interpretation that mitochondrial respiration is dispensable for normal Drosophila NSCs (Homem et al., 2014) contrasts with the clear requirement for OxPhos to support cell cycle progression in the Drosophila eye disc (Mandal et al., 2010; Mandal et al., 2005; Owusu-Ansah et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on Drosophila metabolism.

claim: Loss of the transcription factor Prospero (Pros) generates tumours in which differentiating daughter-cells revert to a NSC-like fate.
source: We first examined whether OxPhos is required in tumours generated by loss of the transcription factor, Prospero (Pros) (Caussinus and Gonzalez, 2005; Choksi et al., 2006), in which differentiating daughter-cells revert to a NSC-like fate (Choksi et al., 2006) (Figure 1h).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on Prospero function.

claim: pros tumours are invasive upon transplantation and exhibit genomic instability over time.
source: pros tumours are invasive upon transplantation and exhibit genomic instability over time (Caussinus and Gonzalez, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on Prospero tumours.

claim: RNAi knockdown of complex I (NDUFS1) or complex V (ATPsynα) in NSCs and tumour cells was performed using Worniu-GAL4.
source: We used RNAi to knock down subunits of complex I (NDUFS1) or complex V (ATPsynα) in NSCs and tumour cells with a NSC-specific driver, Worniu-GAL4 (Albertson et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: The complex I RNAi line has been validated previously.
source: The complex I RNAi line has been validated previously (Garcia et al., 2017; Hermle et al., 2017; Owusu-Ansah et al., 2013; Pletcher et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous validation studies.

claim: Expression of the complex V RNAi in NSCs strongly reduced the levels of ATPsynα.
source: expression of the complex V RNAi in NSCs strongly reduced the levels of ATPsynα (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a–c).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in the figure.

claim: Both complex I and complex V RNAi lines caused fragmentation of mitochondria.
source: Both RNAi lines caused fragmentation of mitochondria (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d–f), a known consequence of OxPhos dysfunction in mouse and human cells (Duvezin-Caubet et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data and a citation to literature on mitochondrial morphology.

claim: Mitochondrial fragmentation is a known consequence of OxPhos dysfunction in mouse and human cells.
source: Both RNAi lines caused fragmentation of mitochondria (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d–f), a known consequence of OxPhos dysfunction in mouse and human cells (Duvezin-Caubet et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on mitochondrial dynamics.

claim: Inhibition of OxPhos in pros tumours caused a decrease in tumour growth and an overall reduction in brain size.
source: To our surprise, inhibition of OxPhos through knockdown of mitochondrial complex I or V in pros tumours caused a decrease in tumour growth and an overall reduction in brain size (Figure 1a–c,i).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Inhibition of glycolysis with an RNAi against aldolase had a comparable effect to OxPhos inhibition on pros tumour growth.
source: This result was comparable to the effect observed upon inhibition of glycolysis with an RNAi against aldolase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Neither glycolysis nor OxPhos are sufficient to support brain tumour growth in vivo.
source: This suggests that neither glycolysis nor OxPhos are sufficient to support brain tumour growth in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing both pathways are required.

claim: Constitutive activation of aPKC (aPKC-CAAX) leads to symmetric division of NSCs in the Drosophila brain.
source: Constitutive activation of aPKC (aPKC-CAAX) leads to symmetric division of NSCs in the Drosophila brain (Lee et al., 2006) (Figure 1h)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on aPKC function.

claim: Loss of brat results in dedifferentiation of the progeny of type II NSCs.
source: whereas loss of brat results in dedifferentiation of the progeny of type II NSCs (Bowman et al., 2008) (Figure 1h).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on Brat function.

claim: In both aPKC-CAAX and brat tumours, knockdown of complex I strongly inhibited tumour growth and decreased overall brain size.
source: In both aPKC-CAAX and brat tumours we found that knockdown of the complex I subunit, NDUFS1, strongly inhibited tumour growth and decreased overall brain size (Figure 1d–g,i).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: OxPhos inhibition in tumours was accompanied by a significant decrease in the mitotic index of tumourigenic NSCs.
source: This was accompanied by a significant decrease in the mitotic index of tumourigenic NSCs (Figure 1j), consistent with mitochondrial metabolism playing a key role in regulating the proliferation rate of brain tumour cells.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1j.

claim: There was no obvious increase in apoptosis upon OxPhos inhibition in pros tumours.
source: There was no obvious increase in apoptosis upon OxPhos inhibition in pros tumours, as assessed by TUNEL-staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d–f).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Growth of pros mutant tumours is sustained by a small proportion of highly proliferative stem cells that express Imp.
source: Growth of pros mutant tumours is sustained by a small proportion of highly proliferative stem cells that express Imp (IGF-II mRNA-binding protein) (Genovese et al., 2018; Narbonne-Reveau et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on tumour stem cells.

claim: Imp-positive tumour stem cells self-renew and generate more differentiated Imp-negative tumour cells with limited self-renewal capacity.
source: These tumour stem cells self-renew and generate more differentiated Imp-negative tumour cells with limited self-renewal capacity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tumour hierarchy cited in the manuscript.

claim: After knockdown of complex I, most tumourigenic NSCs in pros and aPKC-CAAX tumours remained Imp-positive and differentiation into Imp-negative cells was reduced.
source: However, after knockdown of complex I by targeted RNAi, most tumourigenic NSCs in pros and aPKC-CAAX tumours remained Imp-positive and differentiation into Imp-negative cells was reduced (Figure 1k,l—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in the figures.

claim: OxPhos inhibition does not lead to more aggressive tumours, but rather slows it down by decreasing the proliferation rate of the tumour cells.
source: Our results suggest that OxPhos inhibition does not lead to more aggressive tumours, but rather slows it down by decreasing the proliferation rate of the tumour cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing reduced proliferation and differentiation.

claim: Inhibition of OxPhos in NSCs throughout development resulted in smaller brains.
source: We found that, as for tumour cells, inhibition of OxPhos in NSCs throughout development resulted in smaller brains (Figure 1i; Figure 2a–d).
evidence: This is supported by brain size measurements shown in the figures.

claim: The smaller brain size upon OxPhos inhibition could not be explained by an overall developmental delay, as larval and pupal body length was similar to controls.
source: This could not be explained by an overall developmental delay, as larval and pupal body length was similar to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by body length measurements shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Inhibition of glycolysis by NSC-specific knockdown of phosphofructokinase (PFK), aldolase or phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK) had no effect on brain size.
source: In contrast, inhibition of glycolysis by NSC-specific knockdown of phosphofructokinase (PFK), aldolase or phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK) had no effect on brain size and knockdown of pyruvate kinase (PyK) only caused a slight reduction (Figure 2d—figure supplement 2a-d and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by brain size measurements shown in the figures.

claim: Knockdown of pyruvate kinase (PyK) only caused a slight reduction in brain size.
source: In contrast, inhibition of glycolysis by NSC-specific knockdown of phosphofructokinase (PFK), aldolase or phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK) had no effect on brain size and knockdown of pyruvate kinase (PyK) only caused a slight reduction (Figure 2d—figure supplement 2a-d and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by brain size measurements shown in the figures.

claim: Complex I or V knockdown did not cause an increase in apoptosis in the VNC of third instar larvae.
source: Complex I or V knockdown did not cause an increase in apoptosis in the VNC of third instar larvae (L3) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2e–k).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Mitotic index and incorporation of EdU were significantly reduced after complex I or V knockdown in NSCs.
source: However, mitotic index (Figure 2e) and incorporation of the S-phase marker 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) (Figure 2f) were significantly reduced, indicating that NSCs rely on OxPhos for proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2.

claim: NSCs rely on OxPhos for proliferation.
source: However, mitotic index (Figure 2e) and incorporation of the S-phase marker 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) (Figure 2f) were significantly reduced, indicating that NSCs rely on OxPhos for proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced mitotic index and EdU incorporation data.

claim: Live imaging of NSCs in the VNC after complex I knockdown confirmed a striking increase in cell cycle time.
source: Live imaging of NSCs in the ventral nerve cord (VNC) after complex I knockdown confirmed a striking increase in cell cycle time: NSC division was rarely observed in a 3 hr time window, whereas control NSCs divided between one and three times (Figure 2g; Figure 2—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 2g and videos.

claim: ATP concentration in NSCs in the L3 VNC was similar between controls and complex V knockdown.
source: ATP concentration in NSCs in the L3 VNC was similar between controls and complex V knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 2g–i).
evidence: This is supported by ATP FRET sensor measurements shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Acute pharmacological inhibition of glycolysis caused a drop in ATP levels that was significantly more rapid and severe in NSCs with prior complex V inhibition.
source: Acute pharmacological inhibition of glycolysis through application of 2-deoxyglucose to ex vivo cultured brains caused a drop in ATP levels in both conditions. However, this drop was significantly more rapid and severe in NSCs with prior complex V inhibition (Figure 1—figure supplement 2g–i).
evidence: This is supported by ATP FRET sensor measurements shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction results in rewiring of NSC metabolism to rely more on glycolysis for ATP production.
source: This suggests that mitochondrial dysfunction results in rewiring of NSC metabolism to rely more on glycolysis for ATP production.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ATP measurements after glycolysis inhibition.

claim: Drosophila NSCs in the larval VNC progress from an early identity marked by cytoplasmic Imp and nuclear Chinmo, to a late identity marked by cytoplasmic Syncrip (Syp) and nuclear Broad.
source: Drosophila NSCs in the larval VNC progress from an early identity marked by cytoplasmic Imp and nuclear Chinmo, to a late identity marked by cytoplasmic Syncrip (Syp) and nuclear Broad (Liu et al., 2015; Maurange et al., 2008) (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on temporal patterning.

claim: Inhibition of OxPhos caused a defect in temporal patterning of larval NSCs.
source: We found that inhibition of OxPhos caused a defect in temporal patterning of larval NSCs.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data for temporal markers.

claim: After knockdown of complex I, one third of NSCs in the VNC failed to downregulate Imp expression.
source: After knockdown of complex I, one third of NSCs in the VNC (32.0 ± 4.0%, mean ± s.e.m., n = 11 VNCs) failed to downregulate Imp expression (Figure 3b-e—figure supplement 1a-c)
evidence: This is supported by quantification of Imp expression shown in the figures.

claim: After complex I knockdown, some NSCs failed to differentiate into Syp-positive NSCs at the end of larval life.
source: and some (9.1 ± 1.4%, n = 14 VNCs) even failed to differentiate into Syp-positive NSCs at the end of larval life (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d–g).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of Syp expression shown in the figure supplement.

claim: OxPhos inhibition caused a delay in the downregulation of the early temporal factors Castor and Chinmo.
source: Immunostaining for other temporal markers (Maurange et al., 2008; Miyares and Lee, 2019) revealed a delay in the downregulation of the early temporal factors Castor and Chinmo, a decreased peak of expression of the switching factor Sevenup, and delayed upregulation of the late temporal factor Broad (Figure 3e—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in the figures.

claim: OxPhos inhibition caused a decreased peak of expression of the switching factor Sevenup.
source: Immunostaining for other temporal markers (Maurange et al., 2008; Miyares and Lee, 2019) revealed a delay in the downregulation of the early temporal factors Castor and Chinmo, a decreased peak of expression of the switching factor Sevenup, and delayed upregulation of the late temporal factor Broad (Figure 3e—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in the figures.

claim: OxPhos inhibition caused delayed upregulation of the late temporal factor Broad.
source: Immunostaining for other temporal markers (Maurange et al., 2008; Miyares and Lee, 2019) revealed a delay in the downregulation of the early temporal factors Castor and Chinmo, a decreased peak of expression of the switching factor Sevenup, and delayed upregulation of the late temporal factor Broad (Figure 3e—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in the figures.

claim: Similar temporal patterning defects were observed after knockdown of other subunits of complex I (NDUFA10, NDUFV1) or V (ATPsynα, ATPsynγ) in the VNC.
source: Similar results were observed after knockdown of other subunits of complex I (NDUFA10, NDUFV1) or V (ATPsynα, ATPsynγ) in the VNC (Figure 3d—figure supplement 1i–m)
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: OxPhos inhibition in the central brain caused temporal patterning defects.
source: and after OxPhos inhibition in the central brain (CB) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1n–p).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: OxPhos inhibition was accompanied by a significant reduction in the number of NSC progeny expressing Broad and lacking Chinmo.
source: Importantly, this was accompanied by a significant reduction in the number of NSC progeny expressing Broad and lacking Chinmo, indicators of late neuronal identity (Figure 3f-h—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in the figures.

claim: OxPhos is required for NSCs to progress from an early to a late temporal fate.
source: We conclude that OxPhos is required for NSCs to progress from an early to a late temporal fate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the temporal patterning data.

claim: Slowing the cell cycle by expression of Myt1, Wee1 or both strongly decreased final brain size.
source: To test directly whether increasing cell cycle length inhibits NSC temporal progression, we slowed the cell cycle by expression of Myt1, Wee1 (Price et al., 2002) or both, which delay the G2/M transition (Figure 4g) and strongly decrease final brain size (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by brain size measurements shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Delaying the G2/M transition did not affect NSC temporal progression.
source: However, this did not affect NSC temporal progression and no Imp-positive NSCs could be detected at the end of neurogenesis (Figure 4d–f,h).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Expression of Dacapo (Dap) or activated Rb (Rbf280) caused many NSCs in the VNC to express Imp continuously.
source: Next, we tested whether inhibition of the G1/S transition affects temporal progression by expression of Dacapo (Dap; the p21/p27/p57 homologue), or an activated form of Rb (Rbf280). Strikingly, many NSCs in the VNC expressed Imp continuously (Dap: 7.8 ± 1.2%, n = 15 VNCs; Rb: 24.2 ± 3.4%, n = 10 VNCs) (Figure 4a–c,h).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of Imp expression shown in Figure 4.

claim: When Dap and Rbf280 were co-expressed, a majority of NSCs remained positive for the early NSC marker Chinmo.
source: When Dap and Rbf280 were co-expressed, a majority of NSCs remained positive for the early NSC marker Chinmo (80.4 ± 1.1%, n = 4 VNCs) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of Chinmo expression shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The block in temporal patterning correlated with the decrease in mitotic index.
source: The block in temporal patterning correlated with the decrease in mitotic index (Figure 4h—figure supplement 1d,e).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Temporal patterning and generation of neuronal diversity are linked to cell cycle progression at the G1/S rather than the G2/M transition.
source: Our data suggest that temporal patterning and generation of neuronal diversity are linked to cell cycle progression and that regulation occurs at the G1/S rather than the G2/M transition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of G1/S vs G2/M delay.

claim: There is growing evidence for cross talk between mitochondrial metabolism and cell cycle progression at the G1/S transition.
source: There is growing evidence for cross talk between mitochondrial metabolism and cell cycle progression at the G1/S transition (Mandal et al., 2010; Mandal et al., 2005; Mitra et al., 2009; Owusu-Ansah et al., 2008; Schieke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on cell cycle regulation.

claim: Complex I knockdown caused an increase in the number of NSCs in G1 and at the G1/S transition.
source: We found an increase in the number of cells in G1 (26.5 ± 1.6%, n = 9 control VNCs vs. 34.9 ± 1.8%, n = 8 complex I RNAi VNCs) and at the G1/S transition (14.5 ± 2.3%, n = 9 control VNCs vs. 24.3 ± 1.7%, n = 8 complex I RNAi VNCs) (Figure 4i–k).
evidence: This is supported by Fly-FUCCI data shown in Figure 4.

claim: OxPhos dysfunction causes activation of the G1/S checkpoint and this results in delayed temporal patterning of NSCs.
source: Our results suggest that OxPhos dysfunction causes activation of the G1/S checkpoint and this in turn results in delayed temporal patterning of NSCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell cycle and temporal patterning data.

claim: Activation of the G1/S checkpoint upon downregulation of OxPhos activity has been observed in various tissues in Drosophila.
source: Activation of the G1/S checkpoint upon downregulation of OxPhos activity has been observed in various tissues in Drosophila (DiGregorio et al., 2001; Mandal et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on cell cycle checkpoints.

claim: In the eye disc, G1/S delay upon complex I dysfunction was caused by increased production of ROS and JNK-pathway activity.
source: In the eye disc, G1/S delay upon complex I dysfunction was caused by increased production of ROS and JNK-pathway activity, while complex IV dysfunction decreased the ATP/AMP ratio and activated the G1/S checkpoint through AMPK and p53 (Mandal et al., 2010; Mandal et al., 2005; Owusu-Ansah et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on eye disc metabolism.

claim: Complex IV dysfunction decreased the ATP/AMP ratio and activated the G1/S checkpoint through AMPK and p53 in the eye disc.
source: In the eye disc, G1/S delay upon complex I dysfunction was caused by increased production of ROS and JNK-pathway activity, while complex IV dysfunction decreased the ATP/AMP ratio and activated the G1/S checkpoint through AMPK and p53 (Mandal et al., 2010; Mandal et al., 2005; Owusu-Ansah et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on eye disc metabolism.

claim: Decreasing ROS does not rescue the proliferation or temporal patterning defects of complex I or V inhibition in NSCs.
source: Our preliminary data suggest that decreasing ROS does not rescue the proliferation or temporal patterning defects of complex I or V inhibition (data not shown)
evidence: This is stated as preliminary data.

claim: Knock down of AMPK or p53 does not rescue the proliferation or temporal patterning defects of complex I or V inhibition in NSCs.
source: and nor does knock down of AMPK or p53 (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as unpublished data.

claim: Clones mutant for ampk in a background where all NSCs express complex I or V RNAi enhanced rather than suppressed the temporal patterning defect.
source: Moreover, clones mutant for ampk in a background where all NSCs continue to express complex I or V RNAi enhanced rather than suppressed the temporal patterning defect (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The adult CNS in Drosophila does not normally contain NSCs.
source: The adult CNS in Drosophila does not normally contain NSCs (Kato et al., 2009; Siegrist et al., 2010; von Trotha et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on Drosophila development.

claim: NSCs stop dividing in the first 20–30 hr after pupariation at which time they differentiate or undergo apoptosis.
source: NSCs stop dividing in the first 20–30 hr after pupariation at which time they differentiate or undergo apoptosis (Figure 3a) (Homem et al., 2014; Ito and Hotta, 1992; Maurange et al., 2008; Siegrist et al., 2010; Truman and Bate, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on NSC termination.

claim: Knocking down complex III or IV subunits in NSCs prevents termination of proliferation at the onset of pupal life.
source: It was previously shown that knocking down complex III or IV subunits in NSCs prevents termination of proliferation at the onset of pupal life (Homem et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: When complex I or V subunits were knocked down, NSCs were maintained into the adult VNC and CB.
source: Similarly, we found that when complex I or V subunits were knocked down, NSCs, identified by Dpn-expression and continued expression of GFP from a NSC-specific GAL4-driver (Worniu-GAL4), were maintained into the adult VNC and CB (Figure 5a-c—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5.

claim: An average of 30.8 ± 3.1 and 20.2 ± 3.3 NSCs persisted into adulthood when complex I or V were inhibited respectively.
source: Of the 133 NSCs in the larval VNC (Birkholz et al., 2015; Lacin and Truman, 2016), an average of 30.8 ± 3.1 and 20.2 ± 3.3 persisted into adulthood when complex I or V were inhibited respectively (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: NSCs that persisted into adulthood after OxPhos inhibition continued to proliferate and generate neuronal progeny.
source: These NSCs continued to proliferate and generate neuronal progeny (Figure 5a-c—figure supplement 1a-j).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in the figures.

claim: NSCs persisted in the adult CB and VNC when the G1/S, but not G2/M, transition was delayed, independent of OxPhos dysfunction.
source: NSCs also persisted in the adult CB and VNC when the G1/S, but not G2/M, transition was delayed, independent of OxPhos dysfunction (Figure 5d-g—figure supplement 1k-n).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Timely cell cycle exit of Drosophila NSCs at the end of neurogenesis depends on normal progression through the larval temporal cascade.
source: Timely cell cycle exit of Drosophila NSCs at the end of neurogenesis was shown to depend on normal progression through the larval temporal cascade (Maurange et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on NSC termination.

claim: Restoring temporal identity by removing Imp at 48 hr or 72 hr ALH significantly decreased adult neurogenesis in NSCs with complex I knockdown.
source: To test this, we restored the temporal identity in NSCs in which complex I was downregulated by removing Imp at 48 hr or 72 hr ALH. Deletion of Imp significantly decreased adult neurogenesis (Figure 5h–k)
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5.

claim: There is a direct relationship between temporal patterning defects and the adult persistence of NSCs upon OxPhos dysfunction.
source: Deletion of Imp significantly decreased adult neurogenesis (Figure 5h–k), consistent with a direct relationship between temporal patterning defects and the adult persistence of NSCs upon OxPhos dysfunction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Imp deletion rescue experiment.

claim: The previously observed defect in termination of NSC proliferation is a consequence of the earlier temporal patterning defects caused by OxPhos dysfunction.
source: Together, our data indicate that the previously observed defect in termination of NSC proliferation is a consequence of the earlier temporal patterning defects caused by OxPhos dysfunction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the temporal patterning and NSC persistence data.

claim: The metabolic requirements of highly proliferative NSCs in the Drosophila brain cannot be met by aerobic glycolysis alone.
source: Here we show that the metabolic requirements of highly proliferative NSCs in the Drosophila brain, as well as the tumour cells they generate upon transformation, cannot be met by aerobic glycolysis alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing both pathways are required.

claim: Drosophila NSCs require OxPhos for proliferation, generation of diversity through temporal patterning, and termination of proliferation.
source: Instead, Drosophila NSCs require OxPhos for key aspects of their behaviour: proliferation, generation of diversity through temporal patterning, and termination of proliferation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by the experimental data.

claim: Respiratory activity may provide an explanation for the strong increase in ROS production that has been observed in NSCs upon hypoxia.
source: Respiratory activity may provide an explanation for the strong increase in ROS production that has been observed in NSCs upon hypoxia (Bailey et al., 2015)
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings and cited literature.

claim: Respiratory activity may provide an explanation for the developmental lethality caused by CNS-specific mutation of the mitochondrial genome.
source: and for the developmental lethality caused by CNS-specific mutation of the mitochondrial genome (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings and cited literature.

claim: OxPhos dysfunction affects both normal NSCs and tumour cells in the brain.
source: While OxPhos dysfunction affects both normal NSCs and tumour cells in the brain, inhibition of glycolysis only affects tumour growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) but not normal brain development (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the differential effects of OxPhos vs glycolysis inhibition shown in the figures.

claim: Inhibition of glycolysis only affects tumour growth but not normal brain development.
source: While OxPhos dysfunction affects both normal NSCs and tumour cells in the brain, inhibition of glycolysis only affects tumour growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) but not normal brain development (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the differential effects shown in the figures.

claim: Upregulation of aerobic glycolysis has been observed in Hipk, EGFR or PDGF/VEGF-induced tumours in the Drosophila wing disc.
source: This is reminiscent of the upregulation of aerobic glycolysis in Hipk, EGFR or PDGF/VEGF-induced tumours in the Drosophila wing disc (Eichenlaub et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2016; Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on wing disc tumours.

claim: Previous findings suggested that OxPhos is dispensable during normal NSC development and in brain tumours, and is only activated at the end of neurogenesis as part of a metabolic switch to induce termination of NSC proliferation.
source: Our results contrast with previous findings suggesting that OxPhos is dispensable during normal NSC development and in brain tumours, and is only activated at the end of neurogenesis as part of a metabolic switch to induce termination of NSC proliferation (Homem et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a citation to previous literature that the current study contradicts.

claim: Sustained OxPhos activity throughout NSC development is required for normal temporal patterning.
source: While our experiments do not directly address whether this metabolic switch takes place, the results provide an alternate interpretation. We find that sustained OxPhos activity throughout NSC development is required for normal temporal patterning.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the temporal patterning data.

claim: Prolonged expression of early temporal markers makes NSCs unresponsive to the developmental cues that govern cell cycle exit.
source: Prolonged expression of early temporal markers makes NSCs unresponsive to the developmental cues that govern cell cycle exit (Maurange et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on NSC termination.

claim: Restoring temporal progression by timely depletion of Imp enhances termination of proliferation in spite of continued OxPhos inhibition.
source: and we show that restoring temporal progression by timely depletion of the early temporal factor Imp enhances termination of proliferation in spite of continued OxPhos inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by the Imp deletion rescue data.

claim: OxPhos-dependent proliferation is required for temporal patterning and differentiation at the G1/S transition of the cell cycle.
source: Our findings thus integrate key aspects of NSC and tumour cell biology (Figure 6) : OxPhos-dependent proliferation is required for temporal patterning and differentiation at the G1/S transition of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: OxPhos enables NSCs to undergo normal aging and to respond to the developmental cues that instruct termination of proliferation.
source: This enables NSCs to undergo normal aging and to respond to the developmental cues that instruct termination of proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal patterning and termination data.

claim: Adult neurogenesis in the subventricular zone of the mammalian brain depends on p57-induced slowing of the cell cycle during embryonic development.
source: Interestingly, adult neurogenesis in the subventricular zone of the mammalian brain depends on p57-induced slowing of the cell cycle during embryonic development (Furutachi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on mammalian neurogenesis.

claim: It is not known whether p57 expression or mitochondrial dysfunction affects the temporal identity of mammalian NSCs.
source: It is not known whether p57 expression or mitochondrial dysfunction also affects the temporal identity of mammalian NSCs.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The effects of G1/S delay on temporal patterning are specific to the G1/S transition: activation of the G2/M checkpoint did not affect temporal patterning or termination of proliferation.
source: Importantly, the effects we observed are specific to the G1/S transition: activation of the G2/M checkpoint did not affect temporal patterning or termination of proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by the differential effects of G1/S vs G2/M delay.

claim: The size and composition of Drosophila NSC lineages are not strictly predetermined but rather controlled by both intrinsic and extrinsic factors.
source: Our results therefore demonstrate that the size and composition of Drosophila NSC lineages are not strictly predetermined (Birkholz et al., 2015) but rather controlled by both intrinsic and extrinsic factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing metabolic effects on lineage composition.

claim: Metabolic differences exist between NSCs in different regions of the brain or at different developmental stages.
source: Single-cell sequencing data indicate that metabolic differences exist between NSCs in different regions of the brain or at different developmental stages (Davie et al., 2018; Genovese et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to single-cell sequencing studies.

claim: OxPhos might constitute a targetable metabolic vulnerability of cancer.
source: Our study indicates that OxPhos might constitute a targetable metabolic vulnerability of cancer.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings.

claim: Small molecule inhibitors of OxPhos are currently being developed and tested in clinical trials to treat various forms of cancer.
source: Small molecule inhibitors of OxPhos are currently being developed and tested in clinical trials to treat various forms of cancer (Gui et al., 2016; Molina et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2019; Weinberg and Chandel, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on cancer therapeutics.

claim: The in vivo impact of OxPhos dysfunction is much more complex than mere inhibition of proliferation.
source: However, we find that the in vivo impact of OxPhos dysfunction is much more complex than mere inhibition of proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the multiple effects observed beyond proliferation.

claim: A better understanding of the interactions between metabolism, differentiation and tumour heterogeneity in vivo has the potential to uncover novel therapeutic approaches.
source: A better understanding of the interactions between metabolism, differentiation and tumour heterogeneity in vivo has the potential to uncover novel therapeutic approaches.
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the findings.
